content.title: About
content.content: Apricot (Prunus armeniaca) is a small, round stone fruit with velvety, yellow-orange skin and sweet-tart, juicy flesh, native to Central Asia and China. It has a single pit with a kernel inside. Apricots are eaten fresh, dried, or cooked into jams, desserts, and savory dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Apricots are related to peaches, plums, almonds, and cherries.
Dried apricots are a popular snack and are often treated with sulfur dioxide to keep their bright orange color.
Apricots have been cultivated in Central Asia and China for thousands of years.
Apricot kernels contain a compound that can release cyanide, so they should not be eaten raw.
Fresh apricots ripen quickly and are in season for a short time in summer.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Apricots contain beta-carotene, which the body can convert into vitamin A for vision, skin, and immune function.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Apricots contribute fiber, especially when eaten with the skin or dried.

items.title: Contains polyphenols
items.content: Apricots contain plant compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Apricot kernels
items.content: Raw bitter apricot kernels and kernel-based supplements contain a compound that can release cyanide and can be dangerous. Do not eat them.

items.title: Sulfites in dried apricots
items.content: Dried apricots are often treated with sulfites, which can trigger reactions in people with sulfite sensitivity or asthma.

items.title: Natural sugars
items.content: Dried apricots are concentrated in sugar and calories, so portions matter.

items.title: Allergic reactions and digestion
items.content: Some people may be allergic to apricots, and large amounts, especially dried, may cause loose stools.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Apricots can be eaten fresh, sliced into yogurt, oatmeal, and salads, grilled, baked into tarts, or cooked into jams and sauces. Dried apricots can be added to granola, pilafs, stews, and baking. Choose unsulfured dried apricots if you are sensitive to sulfites.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep firm apricots at room temperature until they soften slightly and smell sweet. Ripe apricots can be refrigerated for a few days. Fresh apricot halves can be frozen. Store dried apricots in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, where they keep for several months.

content.title: About
content.content: Cauliflower is a cruciferous vegetable related to broccoli and Brussels sprouts. When quickly cooked in a small amount of oil it stays crisp and develops a mild nutty flavor. It is low‑calorie and packed with nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “cauliflower” comes from the Latin *caulis* (stem) and *flos* (flower), although the vegetable can be white, green, purple or orange.
It was first domesticated in the Mediterranean region more than 7,000 years ago.
Vitamin C is better retained with short‑heat methods such as sautéing.
Cauliflower contains glucosinolates that may support the body’s detox pathways.
In Japan, cauliflower is often used in tempura, where it is briefly deep‑fried in a light batter.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is important for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Good source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A serving of sautéed cauliflower provides about 70–90 kcal, making it diet‑friendly.

items.title: Provides antioxidants
items.content: Compounds like glucosinolates help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Cruciferous allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergic reaction to cauliflower.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: High intake of oxalates can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Added fat during cooking
items.content: Using too much oil can increase the calorie count of the dish.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sautéed cauliflower works as a side dish, can be tossed into salads, pastas, grain bowls, or used in vegetarian tacos. Choose oils with a high smoke point such as olive or canola oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh cauliflower in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, loosely wrapped in a perforated bag, for up to 5 days. Cooked sautéed cauliflower should be consumed within 2–3 days and stored in an airtight container in the fridge.

chicken-and-vegetable-entree-with-rice-d.title: Chicken and Vegetable Entree with Rice (Diet Frozen Meal)

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken and vegetable entree with rice is a diet frozen meal that contains tender chicken breast, a mix of carrots, broccoli and cauliflower, and steamed rice. The dish is designed for quick microwave heating and fits a controlled‑calorie diet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The meal was formulated with dietitian input to keep calories low without sacrificing flavor.
Chicken is flash‑frozen to preserve nutrients.
Vegetables are cut into small pieces for even microwave heating.
Whole‑grain rice is used, increasing the fiber content.
One serving provides about 250 kcal, making it a convenient diet option.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken breast supplies high‑quality protein essential for maintaining muscle mass.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The meal contains minimal saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and whole‑grain rice provide vitamins B6 and B12, important for metabolism.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables and rice
items.content: Helps maintain normal digestive function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain rice raises blood sugar slowly, suitable for glucose control.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: People monitoring salt intake should note the moderate sodium level in the meal.

items.title: Must be fully heated
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave harmful bacteria; follow the recommended heating time.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Microwave the frozen meal according to the package instructions (typically 3–4 minutes on high), stir, and let stand for 1–2 minutes. Optional: add fresh herbs or a splash of soy sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the meal frozen at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours and do not refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Hollandaise sauce is a classic French emulsified sauce made from egg yolks, melted butter, and lemon juice. It has a smooth buttery flavor with a subtle tang and is commonly served with vegetables, fish, seafood, and eggs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: It is one of the five "mother" sauces of French cuisine, alongside béchamel, velouté, tomato, and espagnole.
Traditionally prepared in a double boiler to prevent the eggs from curdling.
The name derives from a Dutch trader who introduced the recipe to Paris in the 17th century.
Variations include Béarnaise sauce, which replaces lemon juice with vinegar and tarragon.
Classic Hollandaise is often served over Eggs Benedict.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Egg yolks provide vitamin B12 and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Butter supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health in moderation.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D from butter aids calcium absorption and bone health.

items.title: Lemon juice adds vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C acts as an antioxidant and supports the immune system.

items.title: High calorie and fat content
items.content: The sauce is rich and calorie‑dense, so it should be consumed in moderate portions, especially on low‑fat diets.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Raw egg yolks can harbor salmonella; use pasteurized eggs or heat the sauce to at least 70 °C.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or dairy
items.content: Individuals with egg or dairy allergies should avoid the sauce or use suitable substitutes.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve warm Hollandaise over asparagus, steamed vegetables, fish (especially salmon), seafood, or as the topping for Eggs Benedict. It can be kept warm for up to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally to maintain the emulsion.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. When reheating, use a double boiler and stir continuously to preserve the emulsion.

content.title: About
content.content: Meatballs NS are a ready‑to‑eat product made from ground meat (beef, pork or a blend) seasoned with aromatic spices and served with sauce (1265). They heat quickly and work as a main dish or a side to various accompaniments.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meatballs are a staple in many cuisines, from Italian “polpette” to Swedish “köttbullar”.
Sauce (1265) is a proprietary tomato‑based sauce with hints of basil and garlic, created especially for NS meatballs.
The product is thermally processed at 80 °C, ensuring safety while preserving juiciness.
Meatballs can be stored frozen for up to 12 months without loss of flavor.
A 150 g serving provides roughly 250 kcal, fitting well into a balanced diet.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat base supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef and pork contain heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meatballs provide B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: Ideal for low‑carb diets as the primary component is meat.

items.title: Beneficial plant additives
items.content: Sauce (1265) includes tomatoes and basil, rich in antioxidants.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beef or pork.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauce (1265) contains salt; people monitoring sodium intake should account for it.

items.title: Requires thorough heating
items.content: Insufficiently heated meatballs may harbor harmful bacteria.

items.title: Calorie density in large portions
items.content: Consuming overly large servings can lead to excess calorie intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meatballs in the microwave (2‑3 min) or on a skillet, drizzle with sauce (1265) and serve with a side such as mashed potatoes, rice, or a vegetable salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen meatballs in a freezer at –18 °C. Once thawed, use within 24 hours and do not refreeze.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-and-s.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce and Seafood

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with cream sauce and seafood is a home‑cooked recipe that combines the nutritional benefits of whole‑grain wheat, the richness of a creamy sauce, and the fresh flavor of seafood. Made from whole‑grain flour, it retains more fiber and micronutrients than traditional white pasta.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta provides roughly twice the dietary fiber of regular white pasta.
A cream sauce made with real cream and a touch of butter enhances the aroma of the seafood.
Seafood such as mussels, shrimp, and squid are rich in omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health.
In Italy, pasta with seafood is traditionally served in summer when fresh catch is abundant.
Preparing the dish at home lets you control salt and fat levels for a healthier meal.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supplies dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion and stable blood sugar.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood provides EPA and DHA, which reduce inflammation and support brain function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cream and seafood contain B12, niacin, and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish offers iron, zinc, and selenium, which contribute to immune health and skin integrity.

items.title: Lower glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta has a lower GI than white pasta, helping to control appetite.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels, or squid.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: The cream sauce adds saturated fat; those monitoring fat intake should use it sparingly.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: If the sauce is made with stock cubes or added salt, sodium can become elevated.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Fresh seafood must be thoroughly rinsed and kept cold to prevent bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the cream sauce and seafood. Garnish with fresh basil, a squeeze of lemon, and grated Parmesan for extra flavor. The dish is best eaten with a fork and spoon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry whole‑grain pasta in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked sauce and seafood should be refrigerated and consumed within 2 days. Reheat gently, adding a splash of cream to keep the sauce silky.
